title: 2013 Report on Studying Abroad at Tulane University
paragraphs: From mid-April 2013, I was given the opportunity to do clinical clerkships at Tulane University in New Orleans in the United States. New Orleans is one of the leading tourist cities of the South, where a festival is held somewhere almost every week, and the medical school and university hospital are located a few minutes' walk from the downtown, which is especially lively even by its standards. I stayed in the student dormitory attached to the university hospital, which was very close to both the hospital and the downtown, so I was able to enjoy my clerkships while savoring the city of New Orleans.

In the first month I rotated through hematology/oncology. The consult team I was assigned to was a small team, at first three people including me. My daily work was to go to the ward in the morning, check the data of my assigned patients, take the history and physical findings, and present to the senior doctors on rounds, and in addition there were conferences, review meetings and lectures for residents, so every day was packed. On rounds I could see truly varied patients, from hematopoietic diseases to solid tumors. The fellow who was in charge of me was a very educational person, who actively threw questions at me during rounds and while moving between places, and carefully taught me when I did not know. I was also allowed to give many presentations on papers and specific topics. I almost laughed a little when I was handed a paper and told "Enjoy!" Since it was the first department I rotated through, there were many hard things. In an unfamiliar environment, my English and medical knowledge were still far from sufficient, and at first I found rounds quite painful. To make up for the shortfall, I prepared thoroughly in advance for the patients to be seen on rounds, wrestling with charts that could hardly be called tidy, and made a point of asking questions on my own initiative. Because I was the only student, it was honestly a month with no rest for my mind, but I think what I gained was very large.

In the second month I rotated through neurology. Together with 伊藤, who studied abroad with me, I was again assigned to a consult team. Three local students also rotated on the same team, and there were many students on other teams as well, whom we joined at lectures, so unlike the previous month I was able to rotate in a lively and fun atmosphere. Because I saw patients together with local students, it was not a case of being alone as in hematology, but I was actually allowed to present on rounds, and I was assigned oral presentations on diseases and other topics just like the local students. There were also clerkships at the stroke center and the charity hospital, where I was able to examine actual outpatients. Rotating with local students for the first time, I felt that the students there are indeed very strong not only in basic knowledge but also in their ability to access data and in presentation skills. Seeing patients every day and independently resolving the questions that arose with reference to Up To Date and sometimes even papers, I thought they were really something, and their presentations were ones that "the audience can listen to comfortably," from which I learned a great deal.

By studying abroad at Tulane University, I was able to meet many people I could never have met if I had stayed in Japan, and I think that by listening to their stories I became able to think about my own future with a broader perspective. At first I agonized greatly over whether I should go abroad or not, and even after it was decided, there were times when I nearly lost heart over how hard the preparation was. And during my stay too, it was by no means all fun and there was a lot that was hard. But looking back now, I think that in exchange I undoubtedly gained valuable experience and happy memories. I cannot thank enough everyone at the International Exchange Office, everyone in the Academic Affairs Division, the professors and seniors who looked after me in the pre-departure training, the fellow students who studied abroad with me, and my parents who supported me financially. Thank you very much.
